At badminton practice in the school sports hall, Lakshmi saw Rakesh miss an easy shuttle and burst out laughing. "Did you see that? He swings like a grandmother with a broom!" she called to the girls on the bench. They laughed. Rakesh went red.
All week she kept it up: his squeaky shoes, his hair gel, the way he said "fantastic" about everything. Whenever he was on court, she was the loudest person in the hall.
On Friday, during water break, her friend Sangeeta sat down beside her. "You talk about Rakesh a lot for someone who can't stand him."
Lakshmi rolled her eyes, grabbed her bottle and marched off to refill it, even though it was still full. Her ears were burning.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi say about the way Rakesh swings?
qa.a: He swings like a grandmother with a broom.

qa.q: Why might mocking Rakesh feel safer to Lakshmi than being friendly to him?
qa.a: Loud teasing makes sure no one, including her, sees that she likes him; her burning ears and the full bottle suggest Sangeeta hit the truth.

qa.q: What choice could Lakshmi make the next time Rakesh is on court?
qa.a: Drop the loud jokes and say something ordinary, even just 'nice shot', which is kinder without exposing her feelings to everyone.

qa.q: How might Rakesh experience a week of Lakshmi's teasing?
qa.a: He probably feels embarrassed and picked on, with no idea she might like him; going red shows it stings.

grounding: A teenage girl who likes a boy mocks him loudly at badminton practice, and a friend's remark makes her flush and walk away.

passage:
Tanvir,
I'm writing this because I can't say it in class with everyone watching. For three weeks I've been making fun of you in front of Pinky and the other girls: your heart diagram in bio practical, your voice cracking in the boys' line at assembly, the way you hold your pen. I laughed the loudest every time.
I think I did it so nobody would guess that I actually look forward to bio practical because you're my lab partner, the only boy who ever lends me his eraser. Even I didn't want to know that. Being mean felt safer than being obvious.
You didn't deserve any of it. I'm sorry. You don't have to reply. I'll stop.
Sudha (the girl who sits behind you)
P.S. Your heart diagram was actually the best one in the class.

qa.q: What did Sudha tease Tanvir about?
qa.a: His heart diagram in bio practical, his voice cracking at assembly, and the way he holds his pen.

qa.q: Why did being mean feel 'safer than being obvious' to Sudha?
qa.a: Teasing hid that she liked Tanvir, so no one, not even Sudha herself, had to face that feeling in front of the others.

qa.q: Which choice in the letter is the real turning point?
qa.a: Naming why she teased, apologising and promising to stop, rather than just going quiet, which gives Tanvir a clear repair.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel reading this letter after three weeks of teasing?
qa.a: Surprised and perhaps relieved, maybe a little awkward about the crush, but able to see the teasing was never about him being worse than anyone.

grounding: A teenage girl writes to the boy she has been mocking in front of friends, admitting the teasing hid that she likes him.

Okay, don't laugh, but I think I've been a jerk to Kalyani. You know she's in our tuition batch? Every time she answers a question, I say something like, "Oh wow, the professor has spoken," and the boys at the back crack up. Yesterday she wore this yellow kurta and I said she looked like a traffic signal. Everyone laughed. She didn't. She just packed her bag early and left.
Then I went home and kept replaying her face. My sister asked why her little brother, the great Arnab, was so grumpy at dinner. The thing is, I don't actually think Kalyani is annoying. I think she's the smartest person in that room, and I... like her. There, I said it. And the only way I know how to be around her is to make fun of her, because then nobody guesses. That's stupid, right?

qa.q: What did Arnab say about Kalyani's yellow kurta?
qa.a: That she looked like a traffic signal.

qa.q: Why does Arnab keep replaying Kalyani's face after tuition?
qa.a: He feels guilty and embarrassed; he likes her, and seeing her hurt by his joke makes him face what the teasing was hiding. 😔

qa.q: What could Arnab do at the next tuition class?
qa.a: Stop the jokes and quietly apologise to Kalyani for the traffic-signal comment, without making a show of it.

qa.q: What is it like for Kalyani when her answers get 'the professor has spoken'?
qa.a: She probably feels mocked for being smart and singled out in front of the boys, which could make her speak up less.

grounding: A teenage boy admits aloud that he mocks a girl in his tuition batch in front of friends because he likes her and fears being found out.

passage:
I'm Kavitha, Ayesha's desk-mate in Class 10, so I saw all of it. When Sameer walked in with a new haircut on Monday, Ayesha said loudly, "Who did that, a lawnmower?" The whole back row laughed.
It kept going all week. At the science exhibition she copied the way he explained his solar-cooker model, hands flapping. When he dropped his tray in the canteen, she clapped first.
Here's the odd thing. In the maths notebook she thinks I don't see, his name is written in tiny letters in the margin, twice. And when he said hi to her at the gate on Thursday, she went bright red, said nothing at all, then called him "the lawnmower" again as soon as he'd gone.
I don't know for sure what's going on in her head. But I don't think it's that she can't stand him.

qa.q: What did Ayesha say about Sameer's new haircut?
qa.a: "Who did that, a lawnmower?"

qa.q: Why might mocking Sameer feel safer to Ayesha than being friendly?
qa.a: Teasing him loudly in front of friends hides the crush, so nobody, not even Sameer, can see she likes him, and she avoids feeling exposed.

qa.q: What choice at the gate could Ayesha make differently next time?
qa.a: When Sameer says hi, she could simply say hi back instead of turning it into another joke once he's gone; a small real reply is less risky than it feels.

qa.q: What is the week like for Sameer?
qa.a: Sameer is laughed at over his haircut, his model and a dropped tray, so he probably feels embarrassed and confused, with no idea the person mocking him likes him.

grounding: Shows, through a desk-mate's eyes, a teenager who loudly mocks the boy she likes in front of friends, the opposite behaviour protecting her from exposure.

passage:
Monday. When Pallavi sang at assembly, Himani, sixteen, turned to the girls behind her and did a squeaky imitation. They giggled. Himani's face stayed hot all through first period.
Thursday. Pallavi asked to borrow Himani's chemistry notes. "Can you even read?" Himani said, loud enough for the row to hear, and tossed them across. Later, alone at the bus stop, she replayed Pallavi's small "thanks" about fifty times.
Next Tuesday. Pallavi stopped by her desk. "Did I do something to you?"
Himani opened her mouth for a joke, and nothing came. "No," she said finally, quietly. "You didn't. Sorry. I'm just... weird around you."
Pallavi blinked, then half smiled. "Okay. Weird is fine. Mean isn't."

qa.q: What did Himani say when Pallavi asked to borrow the chemistry notes?
qa.a: "Can you even read?", loud enough for the row to hear.

qa.q: What does Himani replaying Pallavi's "thanks" at the bus stop reveal?
qa.a: It reveals that Himani cares a lot about what Pallavi thinks; the mocking in front of others protects a crush she feels too exposed to show.

qa.q: What choice on the next Tuesday changed things between them?
qa.a: Himani dropped the joke and quietly admitted that Pallavi hadn't done anything wrong, which let Pallavi answer honestly 🙂

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt before asking, "Did I do something to you?"
qa.a: Pallavi was probably hurt and confused by the teasing, wondering what had gone wrong, and it took courage to ask directly.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager with a crush who mocks the person in front of friends to avoid feeling exposed, until a direct question makes her drop the act.
